title: Enterprise LLM Token Economics
subtitle: What a token is, how token spend spirals out of control, and how enterprises govern it.

scenes.narration: Enterprise LLM token economics. What a token is, how token spend spirals out of control, and how enterprises govern it. About three and a half minutes.

beats.text: Enterprise LLM Token Economics
Tokenomics: the concept, the failures, and the enterprise playbook.
~3.5 minutes

scenes.narration: Start with the unit of account. Models are billed by the token — a chunk of text, roughly four characters. Your prompt, instructions, history and files are input tokens. The model's reply is output tokens, and output typically costs two to four times more than input.

beats.text: Models are billed by the token.
A token ≈ 4 characters. You pay for input and output separately.
Output tokens cost 2–4× more than input.

scenes.caption: Input tokens are cheap-ish; output tokens are the expensive part

scenes.narration: Here's the catch. The context window holds everything — input and output together — and everything in it is re-sent and re-billed on every call. A long system prompt and a growing history get paid for again, and again, each turn.

beats.text: The context window is re-billed every call.
System prompt + history are re-sent each turn.
By call 20, you've paid for the same prompt ~20×.

scenes.narration: Now scale it. One chat message is one model call. One agent task can be many — industry estimates put agentic work at five to thirty times the tokens of a single chat query. Pilot economics priced on one query don't survive contact with production.

beats.text: Agents are a token multiplier.
1 chat call vs. an agent firing 5–30× the tokens per task.
Pilot math ≠ production math.

scenes.caption: Agentic workflows fire many model calls per user action

scenes.narration: And then it breaks. A widely-cited account describes four agents where an Analyzer and a Verifier ping-ponged with no budget cap and no termination — reportedly running eleven days and burning forty-seven thousand dollars. The team had dashboards. They did not have a stop button.

beats.text: The runaway agent loop.
Analyzer ↔ Verifier, no cap, no termination — reportedly 11 days, ~$47K.
They had dashboards — not a stop button. (vendor-reported)

scenes.caption: No budget ceiling + no termination = a loop that bills until stopped

scenes.narration: And these aren't hypotheticals. In 2026, one enterprise client ran up a five hundred million dollar Claude bill in a single month — because no one set a usage cap. Uber exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April. Microsoft pulled back internal Claude Code licenses after per-engineer costs hit five hundred to two thousand dollars a month. The FinOps Foundation heard members say they were three times over their annual token budget — in April.

beats.text: These are real headlines, not hypotheticals.
~$500,000,000 Claude bill in one month — no usage cap. (Tom's Hardware, Cybernews)
Uber: 2026 AI budget gone by April. Microsoft: pulled Claude Code licenses ($500–$2K/eng/mo).
FinOps Foundation members: "3× over our annual token budget — and it's only April." (TechCrunch)

scenes.narration: The maturing response is FinOps for AI — a recognized practice now with its own working group at the FinOps Foundation. Four pillars: visibility, engineering levers, a control plane, and governance.

beats.text: The answer: FinOps for AI.
Four pillars — visibility, levers, control plane, governance.
Treat token spend as a first-class cost scope.

scenes.narration: The architectural center of gravity is the LLM gateway — a layer between your apps and the model providers. The first job it does is the one the failure stories demand: budget and quota enforcement, before any tokens are spent.

beats.text: The control plane: an LLM gateway.
All model traffic flows through one layer.
First job: enforce budgets before tokens are spent.

scenes.narration: Inside the gateway live the engineering levers. Prompt caching reuses the static prefix — about ninety percent off cached input. Batch APIs run async at roughly half price. And a router right-sizes each request, sending easy work to small models and reserving frontier models for hard tasks — reported to cut cost forty to seventy percent.

beats.text: Then the levers.
Caching (~90% off cached input) · batch (~50% off) · routing (40–70%).
Cheapest model that clears the quality bar.

scenes.narration: The last pillar makes it stick. Meter every call and attribute it to a team, feature, or workflow. Feed that into FinOps: showback so spenders own their bills, forecasting on unit economics, and cross-functional reviews. The core lesson — alerting is not enforcement.

beats.text: Close the loop: attribute and govern.
Meter every call → showback, forecasts, reviews.
Alerting is not enforcement.

scenes.narration: So: tokens are the unit of account, output and re-billed context drive the cost, and agents multiply it until something stops them. Meter every call, route all traffic through a gateway that enforces budgets, turn on caching and batch, right-size models, and govern it as FinOps. Build the system that declines the next call — not just the dashboard that reports the last one.

beats.text: Tokens are the unit. Output + re-billed context + agents drive cost.
Meter every call · gateway that enforces · cache + batch · right-size.
Govern it as FinOps: budgets, showback, forecasts.
Build the stop button — not just the dashboard.
